note: Editorial analysis questions maintained in this repository, grouped by issues shared across OSCAL and issues specific to each approach. Each question includes its reasoning; the OSCAL examples provide evidence without settling the design choices.
intro: These questions identify unresolved design choices, not recommended changes. The analysis distinguishes what the OSCAL examples demonstrate from what remains open across models and approaches.

sections.label: Across all four approaches
sections.intro: Gaps in the models themselves. None is answered by choosing an approach, and each changes what all four can express.

questions.q: Should OSCAL carry this content at all, when XCCDF already does?
questions.why: XCCDF already represents benchmark checklists. OSCAL could carry equivalent content or connect checklist references to implementation and assessment records. These choices produce different artifacts, translation work and maintenance obligations. The OSCAL examples do not establish which boundary best supports interoperable hardening workflows.

questions.q: Where does the metadata that describes a rule go?
questions.why: Rule metadata includes severity, weight, rationale and whether a check is automated or manual. The AWS and DISA OSCAL examples use namespaced properties for severity rather than a dedicated field. Consumers need shared conventions to interpret this content. Which metadata belongs on a rule, and whether shared namespaces or schema fields should carry it, remains open.

questions.q: Where does remediation land?
questions.why: The AWS catalog uses remediation links, while the STIG and CIS assessment plans carry remediation steps. The component-first examples do not carry remediation. These conventions do not provide a dedicated rule-remediation field. OSCAL's plan of action and milestones addresses a particular finding, not a reusable fix for every instance of a condition. Which structure should carry reusable remediation instructions remains open.

sections.label: Catalog-first
sections.intro: The rule is a control in a catalog. What is unsettled is how many documents that produces and where the outcome lands.

questions.q: Do many catalogs converge into one profile and one plan of record, or does each catalog need its own?
questions.why: A single plan of record could answer a profile merging the catalogs that apply to a system. Separate plans could instead answer each catalog. These structures produce different file counts and response locations, and change whether benchmark outcomes sit beside regulatory outcomes. The worked scenario assumes convergence and counts 18 files; the question is whether that structure meets implementation and assessment needs.

questions.q: If OSCAL gained a field for requirement level, how much of this disagreement would be left?
questions.why: OSCAL has no dedicated core field distinguishing shall, should and may. The examples can carry such labels in properties, but consumers need conventions to interpret them. Catalog-first puts benchmark and regulatory controls into the same profile. It remains unclear how much model-placement disagreement concerns binding force rather than document structure, and whether a shared requirement-level field would reduce it.

questions.q: Should a control declare its type, so a regulatory control and a technical hardening control can be told apart?
questions.why: The catalog/profile model can combine regulatory controls with technical hardening controls, but it has no dedicated core field distinguishing those kinds. Tools would need a shared property convention or schema support to report regulatory coverage separately from hardening coverage. This question concerns the kind of requirement, distinct from whether its requirement level is shall, should or may.

questions.q: How should benchmark profiles compose with regulatory profiles as the number of controls grows?
questions.why: Combining benchmark and regulatory controls increases the work of resolving imports, selections, exclusions and parameter values. The question is how tools should compose and maintain those profiles at scale without obscuring which source supplied a requirement or how a tailoring decision changes downstream content.

questions.q: Where should benchmark outcomes be recorded, in SSP implementation claims or assessment results, and how should tools distinguish them?
questions.why: An SSP by-component response describes an implementation claim, while assessment results record evidence and outcomes. A benchmark workflow may need both, but they answer different questions. Tools need to distinguish intended configuration from observed satisfaction and preserve the relationship between the two records.

sections.label: Component-first
sections.intro: The rule sits on the component it configures. Open questions concern runner identification, importing component definitions and tailoring benchmark content.

questions.q: Which component definition carries the tie to the framework, the one holding the rules or the one holding the checks?
questions.why: The control link is inline rather than held in a mapping collection. The software component definition holds rules, while the validation component definition holds checks; those artifacts may have different maintainers. A mapping provider could update either or both. The OSCAL examples do not establish which document should own that relationship or how duplicated mappings would stay consistent.

questions.q: Should assessment platform usage be optional in an assessment plan?
questions.why: An assessment plan may describe a runner as a component, a platform using components, or a tool identified through properties. These alternatives leave open when an explicit assessment platform adds necessary information and when a component reference is sufficient for a consumer to execute or interpret a check.

questions.q: When is an assessment component sufficient, and when is an assessment platform also needed?
questions.why: The OSCAL examples use different combinations of assessment-assets, assessment-platforms and components. They do not establish a shared rule for deciding whether a component alone identifies the runner or a platform must also describe its execution context. A consistent distinction would help consumers interpret equivalent workflows.

questions.q: How should an assessment asset be associated with tasks or activities?
questions.why: A task identifies work to perform, while an assessment asset describes resources available to perform it. The component-first examples do not establish a complete, interoperable association between these structures. The question is which references should identify the runner for a particular task or activity.

questions.q: How should an observation identify the assessment asset that produced it when several assets are declared?
questions.why: An assessment result may declare several assets, so naming an observation's producer requires an unambiguous relationship. The component-first result example does not establish a complete path from observation to producing asset. The open question is how consumers should recover that association without relying on tool-specific assumptions.

questions.q: How should an SSP combine benchmark and vendor component definitions that describe the same system component?
questions.why: A system may use vendor component definitions alongside benchmark component definitions for the same software. Importing both can produce overlapping descriptions, rules and control implementations. It remains open whether an SSP should retain multiple OSCAL components, merge them, or use another convention to represent the single system component consistently.

questions.q: Should desired-state values from benchmark component definitions be replaced with actual-state values in the SSP?
questions.why: Rules describe prescribed configuration, while an SSP records the system owner's implementation claims. Replacing prescribed values with actual values could lose the benchmark baseline; retaining only prescribed values could misrepresent implementation. The question is how to keep the two meanings distinct while preserving the relationship between benchmark requirements and the system.

questions.q: Which benchmark context should enter an SSP, and how should tools filter component-definition content during import?
questions.why: Benchmark content can include rules, parameters, rationale and procedural detail, not all of which serves the same purpose in an SSP. Import tooling needs a policy for retaining or omitting that context. The open issue is how to reduce duplication without losing information needed to interpret an implementation claim.

questions.q: How should component definitions support benchmark selection, exclusions and parameter tailoring?
questions.why: The component-first examples place parameters on proposed rules and set-parameters on control implementations. Those structures address parameter values but do not provide a profile's selection and exclusion workflow. How component definitions should support benchmark tailoring, including the scope and persistence of tailoring decisions, remains open.

questions.q: Should assessment plans or assessment results support importing component definitions with benchmark context?
questions.why: The component-first examples carry check content into an assessment plan through assessment assets. That demonstrates one encoding, not a dedicated import mechanism for all benchmark context. The question is whether plans or results should support such imports directly and which rules, parameters and provenance would need to survive.

sections.label: Assessment-first
sections.intro: The rule is an activity in an assessment plan. The open question concerns tailoring requirements without losing their assessment context.

questions.q: How should assessment-plan benchmarks support tailoring available through catalogs and profiles?
questions.why: Activities and steps have no parameter assembly, so the assessment-first examples place required values in text. Tailoring can therefore require editing procedural content rather than selecting controls or setting parameter values through a profile. The question is how to support reusable, auditable tailoring without losing the assessment workflow.

sections.label: Executable-first
sections.intro: The check's code travels in the OSCAL document. What is unsettled is which construct carries it, where it may sit, who may put code there, who owns the vocabulary that runs it, and what the executor matches against.

questions.q: Does a future version add a typed assembly for the executable, or standardise the props on the released part?
questions.why: Two constructs carry code today. A typed assembly, the Rules construct, gives a validator the executor fields themselves and needs a version to ship; the released assessment-method part validates now and gives a validator nothing beyond the existence of a prop. The start page's section 6 states the trade aspect by aspect. Which side a future version takes decides whether the vocabulary lives in the schema or beside it, and neither the concept note nor the published proposal has been put to the Foundation as a schema change.

questions.q: Which assemblies may carry an executable: a part on a control, an implemented requirement, a by-component, an activity?
questions.why: In 1.2.1 a part sits on a control and nowhere else, so the released construct is bound to the control layer, and an implemented requirement, a by-component and an activity have props, links and a description but no parts. The Rules construct sits wherever its schema puts it, on a component in both instances so far. Each home couples the code to something different, a requirement, a platform, or one assessment. The grid in section 6 shows two of six cells occupied.

questions.q: How does an executable on a control reach the system's plan of record?
questions.why: A check on a component reaches the system security plan through by-component, where the system's own responses live. A check on a control reaches it only through the profile the plan imports, and nothing on the by-component names the objective the check tests, which is why question 6a, how a system says it satisfies the rule in its own words, is the fourth approach's weakest cell. Whether a by-component may name an objective, or a part may sit on an implemented requirement, is the same question from the implementation layer.

questions.q: Who may put executable code on a control, and who signs it?
questions.why: A catalog or profile carrying executable methods is code, and an executor that resolves a profile from a URL and runs what it finds has installed a remote code path into every assessed system. The concept note asks for pinned hashes on every rlink, signed catalogs and profiles, an executor that refuses anything unverified, and read-only checks with remediation in a part of its own. None of that is agreed anywhere yet, and nothing in OSCAL distinguishes a part that describes from a part that executes.

questions.q: Who owns the vocabulary of platform, language, evaluation and pass condition?
questions.why: The five props carry everything an executor needs, and every one of them is a convention in a placeholder namespace. The note proposes Metaschema external constraints to hold the enumeration, the way FedRAMP holds its own vocabulary without forking the model, and names no body to publish them. Until one does, two vendors can ship two incompatible checks for one control and the profile author picks.

questions.q: What on a system security plan component does the platform CPE match against?
questions.why: The note matches the platform prop against the component in the plan of record, the way XCCDF matches its platform element. No field on an OSCAL component or inventory item carries a CPE, so the match is made on a convention the note leaves open, and it says itself that a plain token may serve as well. Which host a check runs on is decided wherever that convention is decided.

questions.q: Does a finding resolve to an objective that only a profile added?
questions.why: The mechanism rests on findings targeting an objective id, and the objective exists only in the resolved profile: the catalog it imports has never heard of it. A consumer reading the result against the catalog alone, or against a profile resolved without the tool vendor's additions, finds no such objective. Whether every result reader resolves the profile first is not established.

questions.q: When a guide ships as a catalog with its own checks, does a mapping collection carry its tie to the framework?
questions.why: The note answers the framework case by placement: a profile adds the check to the framework control, and the placement is the tie. Where the guide is its own catalog the note supplies no tie. The generated corpus turns the benchmark's own SP 800-53 references into a mapping collection, which reaches controls and statements and not parts, so it ties the recommendation and not the objective beside it. Whether that is the route the note intends is open.

questions.q: Is a changed check a new version of the catalog it sits in?
questions.why: The note accepts the coupling: a changed check is a new profile version, and a catalog that ships checks changes whenever one of them does. A benchmark already carries that coupling in its source material. A framework catalog does not, and the approach keeps it out of one by putting the checks in a profile, so the question is only open for the catalog route.

questions.q: How does a parameter reach a script that expects a fixed variable name?
questions.why: The note exports every param on a control as an environment variable named after the param id. CIS-CAT's scripts read one variable, XCCDF_VALUE_REGEX, and OSCAL parameter ids are unique across a document, so the 82 controls that export a value cannot each declare a parameter of that name. The generated corpus carries the variable's name as the parameter's class, and the note's convention has no answer for it yet.
